clinicalPearls: Xanthelasma palpebrarum presents as soft, symmetrical, yellowish plaques on the eyelid skin, most often at the medial canthus of the upper lids, and is the commonest cutaneous xanthoma.
Roughly half of affected patients have normal serum lipids, so a normolipidaemic result does not exclude the diagnosis, but a fasting lipid profile should still be checked in all cases.

When associated with dyslipidaemia it typically reflects raised low-density lipoprotein or a reduced high-density lipoprotein, and may be a clue to familial hypercholesterolaemia, especially with young onset or a family history.
Xanthelasma has been linked to increased cardiovascular risk independent of measured lipids, so its presence warrants overall cardiovascular risk assessment, not merely a cosmetic view.
The lesions are benign and mainly a cosmetic concern; treatment options include surgical excision, chemical cautery, ablative laser and cryotherapy, all with a notable tendency to recur.
Recurrence after treatment is common, particularly in patients with persistent hyperlipidaemia, so lipid control and patient counselling about recurrence are integral to management.
Consider secondary causes of hyperlipidaemia such as diabetes, hypothyroidism, cholestatic liver disease and nephrotic syndrome when xanthelasma is florid or of early onset.
Eruptive or tuberous xanthomas elsewhere, or extensive early xanthelasma, should prompt evaluation for a primary lipid disorder.
reference.pathophysiology: Xanthelasma results from accumulation of lipid-laden macrophages (foam cells) in the superficial dermis of the thin eyelid skin. Circulating lipoproteins, particularly low-density lipoprotein, extravasate through leaky periocular capillaries and are taken up by dermal macrophages, which become engorged with cholesterol and cholesteryl esters to form perivascular and periadnexal foam-cell aggregates. Local capillary permeability, oxidative modification of lipoproteins and macrophage scavenger-receptor activity all contribute, which explains why lesions can develop even in normolipidaemic individuals in whom local rather than systemic factors predominate.
additionalDifferentials: Necrobiotic xanthogranuloma (often with periorbital induration and paraproteinaemia)
Sebaceous hyperplasia or sebaceous gland carcinoma
Adult-onset asthma and periocular xanthogranulomatous disease (Erdheim-Chester, adult xanthogranuloma)
additionalInvestigations: Fasting serum lipid profile (total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, triglycerides)
Fasting glucose or HbA1c to screen for diabetes
Thyroid function tests to exclude hypothyroidism
Liver function tests to exclude cholestatic liver disease
Assessment for familial hypercholesterolaemia including family history and, where indicated, genetic evaluation
Skin biopsy only if the diagnosis is atypical or xanthogranulomatous disease is suspected
redFlags: Early-onset or florid lesions suggesting familial hypercholesterolaemia
Associated periorbital induration, ulceration or systemic features suggesting necrobiotic xanthogranuloma and paraproteinaemia
Rapidly enlarging, firm or ulcerated eyelid lesion raising concern for sebaceous carcinoma
Features of undiagnosed diabetes, hypothyroidism or cholestasis on systemic enquiry
reference.prognosis: Benign with no direct threat to vision; the main significance is as a marker of possible dyslipidaemia and cardiovascular risk. Cosmetic treatment is effective but recurrence is frequent, particularly when hyperlipidaemia is uncontrolled.
pitfalls: Assuming normal lipids exclude the diagnosis or obviate cardiovascular risk assessment
Treating the lesions cosmetically without addressing underlying dyslipidaemia, leading to recurrence
Mislabelling necrobiotic xanthogranuloma or sebaceous carcinoma as simple xanthelasma
Aggressive excision of medial canthal lesions risking cicatricial ectropion or canthal webbing
Neglecting to screen for secondary causes such as hypothyroidism and cholestasis
references: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology: A Systematic Approach
